title: Birds around us: feathers, beaks, nests and calls

summary.text: Every bird has feathers, and no other animal alive today has them. A hen is a bird, and a bat is not. Birds use their beaks as tools, build nests for their eggs, and call to each other all day long. Your child sits at the window at three times of one day and drops a bean in a cup for every bird call they hear. Then you compare the cups to see when the birds call most, and talk about what the calls mean.
summary.art: A city balcony with a crow on the railing, a bulbul in a potted plant, a pigeon on an AC box, and a girl dropping beans into a steel cup.

intro.hook: Close your eyes at the window for one minute. How many birds can you hear?
intro.text: Even in a big city, birds call outside almost every window. You may hear a crow, a myna, a pigeon or a koel. Count the calls on your fingers. In this unit we find out what birds are, and what their calls mean.
intro.art: A girl with her eyes shut at an open window, counting on her fingers, with a crow and a myna on a wire outside.

outcomes: By the end I can say what makes a bird a bird: feathers.
By the end I can say two jobs that feathers do.
By the end I can say how a beak fits the food a bird eats.
By the end I can say why birds build nests, and name two kinds of nest.
By the end I can listen, count bird calls with beans, and say what I found.
By the end I can say how to feed and give water to birds safely.

terms.meaning: A bird is an animal with feathers. Every bird has a beak, two wings and two legs, and lays eggs.
terms.example: A crow, a hen, a peacock and an ostrich are all birds.
terms.art: A crow, a hen, a peacock and an ostrich standing in a row, with their feathers drawn clearly.

terms.meaning: A feather is a light, strong part that grows out of a bird's skin, as hair grows out of yours.
terms.example: A pigeon has stiff feathers on the wings and soft, fluffy feathers close to the body.
terms.art: A long stiff wing feather next to a small fluffy feather, both grey, on a white page.

terms.meaning: A beak is a bird's hard mouth. Birds have no teeth. The beak picks up, holds and breaks the food.
terms.example: A parakeet cracks a hard seed with a strong, hooked beak.
terms.art: A green parakeet holding a seed in her red hooked beak.

terms.meaning: A nest is a safe place a bird makes to lay eggs and keep the chicks.
terms.example: A crow builds a nest of sticks high in a tree.
terms.art: A crow sitting on a nest of sticks in the fork of a tree, with a bit of wire woven in.

terms.meaning: A call is a short sound a bird makes to send a message. A song is a longer string of sounds.
terms.example: A crow calls 'kaa' to other crows. A koel sings 'ku-oo, ku-oo', louder and louder.
terms.art: A crow with a short sound line and a koel with a long wavy sound line coming from the beaks.

explanations.concept: What makes a bird a bird
explanations.definition: A bird is an animal with feathers. Today, only birds have feathers.
explanations.description: Many people think a bird is any animal that flies. But a bat flies and has fur, not feathers. A bat is not a bird. A hen can only flap a short way, and an ostrich cannot fly at all, but both have feathers. So they are birds.
examples: A hen is a bird. She has feathers.
A bat is not a bird. A bat has fur.
A butterfly is not a bird. A butterfly is an insect.
explanations.context: This card says what every bird has, and no other animal alive today has.
explanations.art: A hen with feathers on one side, and a bat with furry body and thin skin wings on the other.

explanations.definition: Feathers help a bird fly, keep warm, keep dry and show colours.
explanations.description: Stiff feathers on the wings push on the air, so the bird can fly. Soft, fluffy feathers near the skin hold warm air close to the body. Each feather has tiny hooks that zip the strands together. A bird combs and zips her feathers with her beak every day.
examples: A pigeon on a winter morning looks round and fat, because the feathers are fluffed up.
A peacock shows his long, shining tail feathers.
Birds drop old feathers and grow new ones. That is why we find feathers on the ground.
explanations.context: This card says what feathers do for a bird.
explanations.art: A pigeon fluffed up round on a cold ledge, next to the same pigeon thin and sleek on a hot day.

explanations.concept: A beak is a tool for the food
explanations.definition: The shape of a bird's beak fits the food that bird eats.
explanations.description: A sparrow has a short, thick beak to crack small seeds. A sunbird has a long, thin, curved beak to reach the sweet juice deep in a flower. A kingfisher has a long, sharp beak to catch fish. A crow has a strong beak for almost any food. You can guess what a bird eats by looking at the beak.
examples: A sparrow cracks grains with a short, thick beak.
A purple sunbird sips nectar with a long, curved beak.
A kingfisher catches a fish with a long, sharp beak.
explanations.context: This card says how a bird's beak fits the bird's food.
explanations.art: Four bird heads side by side: a sparrow, a sunbird, a kingfisher and a crow, each with their food beside them.

explanations.concept: Nests are for eggs and chicks
explanations.definition: A bird builds a nest to keep the eggs and chicks safe and warm.
explanations.description: Most birds do not live in a nest all year. They build one when it is time to lay eggs. Each kind of bird builds in their own way. A crow uses sticks, and in cities sometimes wire. A tailorbird stitches two leaves together with thread from plants or spider silk. A pigeon makes a small pile of twigs on a ledge.
examples: A crow's nest of sticks sits high in a tree.
A tailorbird's nest hides inside two leaves stitched together.
A red-wattled lapwing lays her eggs on bare ground, and sometimes on a flat roof.
explanations.context: This card says why birds build nests, and how different birds build them.
explanations.art: Three nests: a crow's stick nest in a tree, a tailorbird's leaf cone, and a pigeon's few twigs on a window ledge.

explanations.description: Birds call to tell other birds things. One call can mean 'danger, a cat is near'. Another can mean 'here is food' or 'where are you?'. Birds sing to say 'this place is mine' and to find a partner. Other birds act on these calls, so the calls are messages. Some scientists say only humans have a real language, and bird calls are simpler signals.
examples: Crows call loudly together when they see a cat or an owl.
A koel calls again and again in the hot months before the rains.
A chick calls when hungry, and the parents bring food.

perspectives.explanation: Birds talk to each other. Japanese tits even put two calls together in a set order, and other tits understand the order.
Bird calls carry a few messages, like danger or food. Only humans put words together to say endless new things.

explanations.context: This card asks what birds are saying when they call.
explanations.art: Three crows on a wire calling loudly at a cat on a wall below, with sound lines from their beaks.

explanations.definition: Birds need clean water every day, and the right food if we feed them.
explanations.description: In an Indian summer, city birds can find it hard to get water. A shallow bowl of clean water helps them drink and bathe. Change the water every day, so mosquitoes cannot breed in it. If you put out food, give grains, plain cooked rice or cut fruit. Never give salty, spicy, sugary or fried food.
examples: A clay bowl of water on a balcony in May.
A pinch of broken rice or millet on a ledge.
No namkeen, chips or biscuits for birds.
explanations.context: This card says how to help birds near your home without harming them.
explanations.art: A shallow clay bowl of water on a balcony floor with a myna drinking, and a small plate of grains beside it.

agreed.evidence: Scientists have looked at every kind of animal alive. Birds are the only ones with feathers. Bats, butterflies and flying insects fly without them.

agreed.text: Many birds learn their songs by listening, the way children learn to talk.
agreed.evidence: In the 1950s, William Thorpe raised young chaffinches who never heard a grown-up chaffinch. They grew up singing only a simple, odd song.

agreed.text: Birds call and sing most in the early morning.
agreed.evidence: Bird watchers all over the world hear the loudest singing around sunrise. It is called the dawn chorus.

challenging.claim: A bird is any animal that flies.
challenging.who: A common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Most birds fly, and flying is the first thing we notice about them.
challenging.against: A bat flies but has fur. An ostrich and a penguin cannot fly but have feathers. Feathers make a bird, not flying.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that flying makes an animal a bird.

challenging.claim: If you touch a baby bird, the mother will leave the chick.
challenging.for: People want to stop children from picking up chicks.
challenging.against: Most birds do not leave a chick because a person touched them. But it is still best to leave a chick alone. A chick on the ground is often learning to fly, and the parents are close by.
challenging.context: This card is about a belief many families have about baby birds.

challenging.who: Many families, and some bird scientists who disagree
challenging.for: Water and grain help birds in hot summers and in cities with few trees.
challenging.against: Salty or sugary food can make birds ill. Feeding big flocks of pigeons in one place can push other birds away, and the droppings can make some people ill.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument: does feeding birds always help them?

big_questions.q: A bat flies and an ostrich cannot. Why do we call the ostrich a bird and not the bat?
big_questions.hint: What does an ostrich have that a bat does not have?

big_questions.q: Why do birds call most in the early morning?
big_questions.hint: Scientists still argue about this. Think about what a bird can and cannot do in the dark.

big_questions.q: You learned to talk by listening. A young bird learns to sing by listening. Are we more alike than we look?
big_questions.hint: Think about who you listened to when you were a baby.

big_questions.q: The crows, the pigeons and your family all live in the same building. Whose home is it?
big_questions.hint: Who was here first? Who uses which part?

story.title: The Bulbuls in the Money Plant
story.note: Thenmozhi, Arul and Paati are made up. Red-vented bulbuls really do nest in balcony plants in Indian cities, lay two or three spotted eggs, give sharp alarm calls when a cat comes near, and feed their chicks insects and fruit.
text: Thenmozhi lived on the third floor of a flat in Madurai. She was six. Her little brother Arul was four. Their Paati, their grandmother, kept a row of plants on the balcony.
One morning, Paati called softly. "Come and look. But walk slowly."
In the money plant, two brown birds were hopping in and out. Each one had a black cap on the head and a patch of red under the tail. They were red-vented bulbuls.
One bulbul had a dry grass stem in her beak. She pushed the grass in between the leaves. Then she flew away and came back with a bit of soft root.
"They are building a nest," said Paati. "A nest is a cradle for their eggs."
Arul wanted to touch the nest. Thenmozhi held his hand. "If we go too close, they will be frightened," she said. "Let's watch from the door."
For three days the bulbuls worked. The nest became a small, neat cup, like a tiny katori made of grass. Then, one morning, there were two pink eggs inside, with dark spots.
Now one bulbul sat on the eggs almost all day. The other bulbul brought food. The family watered the plants very quietly, and only from the edge.

One afternoon, the neighbour's cat walked along the balcony wall. At once the bulbul on the railing called, sharp and fast. The bulbul on the nest pressed down flat and kept very still. A myna on the next balcony began to scold the cat too.
The cat looked up, looked around, and jumped down.
"Did you hear that?" said Thenmozhi. "That was not singing. That bulbul was shouting, 'Danger! A cat!'"
"How do you know?" asked Arul.
"Because the other bulbul hid as soon as she heard it," said Thenmozhi. "And the myna understood too."
Paati smiled. "Birds talk all day," she said. "We just don't listen."

About two weeks later, the eggs hatched. Out came two tiny chicks with no feathers, only pink skin and big yellow mouths. Whenever a parent landed, the chicks opened their beaks wide and called, "Cheep, cheep, cheep!" That call meant, "Feed me!" The parents pushed small insects and bits of fruit into the open mouths.
Every day the chicks grew. Grey prickles came out on their skin, and the prickles opened into feathers. Soon the chicks filled the whole nest.
Arul made a rule. "No loud music on the balcony," he said. "The babies are sleeping." Thenmozhi said it was the best rule he had ever made.

Then one morning the chicks stood on the edge of the nest. They flapped their short wings. One chick fluttered to the railing. The other followed. The parents called from the neem tree below, again and again. The chicks called back. Then all four bulbuls were gone into the green.
The nest sat empty in the money plant. Arul looked sad.
"Listen," said Thenmozhi. From the neem tree came a bulbul call, and then a small answer.
"They are still talking," said Arul.
That night Thenmozhi drew the nest, the two eggs, the cat and the four bulbuls. Under it she wrote, with Paati's help: "Our balcony is their home too."
story.epiphany: The bulbul's sharp call was a message. The other bulbul and even the myna understood it.
ask: How did Thenmozhi know the bulbul was saying 'danger'?
Why did the family stay away from the nest?
What did the chicks' 'cheep, cheep' mean?
art: Two bulbuls carrying grass into a money plant on a city balcony, with a girl and a small boy watching from the doorway.
A bulbul calling on the railing while a cat walks along the balcony wall, and the other bulbul pressed flat on the nest.
Two fluffy bulbul chicks on the edge of a grass nest, flapping short wings, with the parents calling from a neem tree.

games.title: Bird or Not a Bird? Look for the feathers
games.players: 2 to 4 players: a grown-up and a child, or more
games.context: This is a sorting card game. Each card names an animal or a thing that flies, walks or swims. Players decide if each one is a bird, and the back of the card says why.

items.b: A bird. She has feathers, even though she can hardly fly.

img.credit: Raja Sekhar Chimirala, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Not a bird. A bat flies, but has fur and no feathers.
A bird. An ostrich cannot fly, but has feathers.

img.credit: Andrew Allen, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Not a bird. A butterfly is an insect, with tiny scales on the wings.
A bird. Feathers, a beak, two wings, two legs.
Not a bird. A fly is an insect with six legs and no feathers.

img.credit: Mitul and Vijul Singh, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: A bird. A penguin swims instead of flying, and has feathers.
A bird. His long tail is made of feathers.

img.credit: Parth Kansara, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Not a bird. A paper kite flies, but was never alive.

items.f: Black kite (the brown bird circling over the city)
items.b: A bird. This kite is a bird of prey with feathers. The paper kite is a different thing.
A bird. Her feathers keep her dry in the water.

img.credit: Raja Sekhar Chimirala, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Not a bird. An aeroplane flies, but has no feathers and is a machine.

rules: Put two sheets of paper on the floor. Write BIRD on one and NOT A BIRD on the other.
Mix the cards and put them in a pile, name side up.
Take turns. Take the top card. The grown-up reads the name aloud.
Put the card on BIRD or NOT A BIRD. Say why.
Turn the card over. The grown-up reads the back. If you were right, keep the card in front of you. If you were wrong, put it back at the bottom of the pile and try again later.

When the pile is finished, count your cards. The player with the most cards wins. If two players have the same number, they both win. Then find the two birds that cannot fly at all, and the animals that fly but are not birds.

setup.art: Two sheets on a floor, one labelled BIRD and one NOT A BIRD, with a pile of picture cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the two sheets and the pile of cards.

setup.art: A child putting a bat card on the NOT A BIRD sheet while a grown-up reads the back.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each card and say why. Turn it over to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Lay out the two sheets. 3. Ask your child how they will decide which animals are birds.
flow.say: What makes a bird a bird? How will you decide which cards go on BIRD?
flow.kid: How will you know if an animal is a bird?

ask.q: How will you decide if an animal is a bird?

flow.parent: Most children say 'if it flies'. Don't correct them yet. The game will test that idea.

flow.do: Take turns with the cards. After each card, read the back aloud.
flow.say: Is a hen a bird? She can hardly fly. What does she have that a bat does not?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Bird or not a bird? Say why.

ask.q: Why is the bat not a bird?
Why is the ostrich a bird?
good: She has a beak and feathers.

flow.do: Look at the two piles together. Ask what every card on the BIRD sheet has.
flow.say: Look at all the birds. What does every one of them have?
flow.kid: What do all the birds have?

check.why: A hen has feathers, so she is a bird. A bat has fur, and a butterfly is an insect. Flying does not make an animal a bird.

games.title: Danger Call: a running and freezing game
games.context: This is a moving game about alarm calls. Players are birds pecking for food. When the lookout bird gives the danger call, every bird flies to safety or freezes.

items.b: Call 'pit-pit-pit-pit' fast. Birds fly to the safe place.
Call one long 'seeee'. Birds freeze and stay still.
Call 'chuk-chuk'. Birds come to the lookout.
Sing a long, happy tune. Birds go back to pecking.
Call 'cheep cheep'. The nearest bird brings you a paper scrap as a pretend worm.

rules: Choose a safe place, like the sofa or a mat. This is the tree.
Tear newspaper into small scraps and scatter them on the floor. These are the seeds.
One player is the lookout bird. The others are birds, pecking up seeds with two fingers. With only two players, there is one lookout and one bird.
The lookout picks a call card and makes that call. The other birds do what the call means.
A bird who does the wrong thing says 'oops' and tries again at the next call.
Each lookout makes three calls, then passes the cards to the next player. Play until every player has been the lookout once.

setup.art: Children crouching on a floor pecking paper scraps with two fingers, with a sofa marked as the tree.
setup.caption: 1. Scatter paper seeds. The sofa is the tree.

setup.art: A girl holding a call card and calling, while the other children run to the sofa.
setup.caption: 2. The lookout calls. The birds fly or freeze.

flow.do: 1. Tear a sheet of newspaper into small scraps and scatter them. 2. Choose the tree. 3. Read the call cards aloud together.
flow.say: Birds use different calls for different dangers. Let's learn the calls first.
flow.kid: Learn the calls. Each call means something different.
flow.parent: These calls are made-up sounds for the game. Real alarm calls differ between kinds of birds, but many small birds do use one call for a danger on the ground and another for a hawk in the sky.

flow.do: Play. The grown-up is the first lookout, then the others take turns. Each lookout makes three calls.
flow.say: Peck, peck, peck. Listen carefully. What is the lookout saying?
flow.kid: Peck the seeds. Listen for the lookout's call. Then act fast.

ask.q: Why did you freeze for the hawk call but run for the cat call?
good: Staying still hides me from a hawk above.
Going up the tree keeps me away from a cat on the ground.

flow.do: Sit down together. Ask why a bird needs more than one danger call.
flow.say: Why do birds need a different call for a cat and for a hawk?
flow.kid: Why does a bird have two danger calls?

check.q: A crow calls loudly and many crows fly to the tree. What could the call mean?
check.why: A loud call that makes other crows act is a message, often about danger. Crows call together when they see a cat or an owl.

experiments.title: A Bean for Every Call: when do birds call most?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sit at a window for 5 minutes at three times of one day: early morning, afternoon and evening. Each time you hear a bird call, you drop one bean into a cup. At the end you compare the three cups.
experiments.question: When do the birds outside our window call most: in the early morning, in the afternoon or in the evening?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which cup will have the most beans: morning, afternoon or evening? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We listen at the same window each time, for the same 5 minutes, with the TV and music off. The same person drops the beans. One bean means one call, or one burst of calls when they come too fast.

materials.item: 3 steel cups or katoris, with paper labels: Morning, Afternoon, Evening
dried beans such as rajma or chana, or buttons (about 70 beans in all)
a phone or clock to time 5 minutes
a window that opens, or a balcony

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays with the child at an open window or on the balcony. Keep the beans away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Early morning, within an hour after sunrise: guess, then listen for 5 minutes and drop the beans.
Afternoon, between 1 and 3 o'clock: listen for 5 minutes and drop the beans.
Evening, about an hour before dark: listen for 5 minutes, then line up the beans and compare.

experiments.record: Draw the three cups. Draw the beans from each cup in a line under it. Draw the birds you heard.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from a flat in Chennai
rows: Yes, the koels called back and forth

setup.art: Three labelled steel cups on a window sill: Morning, Afternoon, Evening, with a small heap of rajma beans.
setup.caption: 1. Label three cups. Put a heap of beans beside them.

setup.art: A girl at an open window with her eyes half closed, dropping a bean into a cup while a grown-up watches a phone timer.
setup.caption: 2. For 5 minutes, drop one bean for every bird call.

setup.art: Three lines of beans on a table, one long, one short and one in between, under the three cups.
setup.caption: 3. Line up the beans from each cup and compare.

flow.do: 1. Label the three cups Morning, Afternoon and Evening. 2. Show your child the beans. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will listen three times today. Which cup do you think will get the most beans? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which cup will get the most beans? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that cup will get the most beans?
good: Birds wake up in the morning.
In the afternoon it is too hot.
Birds go to sleep in the evening.

flow.parent: Write the guess and the reason on a slip of paper and put it under the cup. Don't say what usually happens.

flow.do: 1. Early morning, within an hour after sunrise, sit at the window. 2. Start a 5-minute timer. 3. Your child drops one bean in the Morning cup for every call. 4. Whisper the bird's name if you know it.
flow.say: Shh. Listen. Every time you hear a bird, drop a bean. Did that bird get an answer?
flow.kid: Listen. Drop one bean for each bird call. Is another bird answering?

ask.q: Did one bird call, and then another bird answer?
good: Yes, two crows were calling to each other.
The koel called and another koel called back.

flow.parent: If calls come too fast, drop one bean for each burst of calls. Crows, mynas, pigeons, bulbuls, sparrows, parakeets and, in the hot months, koels are the usual voices. Count only sounds you are sure are birds.

flow.do: In the afternoon, between 1 and 3 o'clock, do the same at the same window with the Afternoon cup.
flow.say: We sit at the same window for the same 5 minutes. Is it louder or quieter than the morning?
flow.kid: Sit at the same window for 5 minutes. Drop one bean in the Afternoon cup for each bird call.

ask.q: Is it louder or quieter than the morning?
good: Only a crow and a pigeon.

flow.parent: Afternoons are often quiet, especially in hot weather, when many birds rest in the shade.

flow.do: About an hour before dark, listen again with the Evening cup.
flow.say: This is the last time we listen. Listen for birds going home to sleep. Are they calling together?
flow.kid: Listen one last time. Drop one bean in the Evening cup for each bird call.
flow.parent: In many Indian cities, crows, mynas and parakeets gather noisily in big trees before dark. Your evening cup may be fuller than you expect.

flow.do: 1. Tip each cup out. 2. Help your child lay the beans from each cup in a straight line, side by side. 3. Count each line together.
flow.say: Let's put the beans in lines. Which line is the longest? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Put each cup's beans in a line. Which line is longest?

ask.q: Which time had the most calls?
good: The morning. That line is the longest.
The evening had more than the afternoon.

flow.parent: Lining up the beans makes a picture graph your child can see at a glance. In most homes the morning line is longest. If your result is different, that is a real result. Talk about why: rain, traffic or a tree nearby can change the result.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they found, what they saw and why they think it happened.
flow.say: What did you find? What did the beans show? Why do you think the birds called so much at that time?
flow.kid: Tell your grown-up what you found. Why do you think the birds called most at that time?

ask.q: Why do birds call so much in the morning?
good: To find their friends after the night.

flow.think: When one bird called and another answered, what were they saying?

check.q: At what time of day do most birds call the most?
options: In the middle of the night
check.why: Most birds call and sing most around sunrise. Scientists call this the dawn chorus. Some city birds are noisy in the evening too.

activities.title: A Feather Up Close: unzip it and zip it back
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at a real feather. You pull the strands apart and stroke them back together, the way a bird mends a feather with the beak. Do this if you have a feather.

materials.item: a clean feather, such as a craft feather from a stationery shop
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: A feather found outside can carry germs. Use a craft feather, or ask a grown-up to wash a found feather in soapy water and dry it. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Look at a feather. Unzip the strands, zip them back, and blow on the fluffy part.

activities.record: Draw your feather, big. Show the middle stem, the strands, and the fluffy bit at the bottom.

setup.art: A child's fingers gently pulling apart the strands of a grey feather to make a gap.
setup.caption: 1. Gently pull two strands apart to make a gap.

setup.art: A child's fingers stroking the feather from the stem to the tip, closing the gap.
setup.caption: 2. Stroke from the stem to the tip. The gap closes.

flow.do: Give your child the feather. Ask them to touch the stiff middle and the soft strands, and the fluffy part at the bottom.
flow.say: Feel the feather. Which part is stiff? Which part is soft? Which part is fluffy?
flow.kid: Feel the feather. Find the stiff part, the soft part, the fluffy part.

flow.do: 1. Gently pull two strands apart to make a gap. 2. Ask your child to guess if the gap can be closed. 3. Stroke from the stem to the tip.
flow.say: I have made a gap. Can we mend it? What do you think will happen if we stroke it?
flow.kid: Pull two strands apart to make a gap. Now stroke the feather gently from the stem to the tip. What happens?
flow.parent: Each strand has tiny hooks along the side, too small to see without a strong magnifier. Stroking hooks them together again. Birds do this with their beaks every day. Some craft feathers are cut or glued and zip poorly. A pigeon or crow feather picked up from the ground works best, once a grown-up has washed it in soapy water and dried it.

flow.do: Hold the feather by the stem and blow gently on the fluffy part at the bottom.
flow.say: Blow on the fluffy part. Why do you think birds have fluffy feathers close to their skin?
flow.kid: Blow on the fluffy part. Why does a bird need fluff?

ask.q: Why do birds have fluffy feathers?

flow.think: When a pigeon fluffs up on a cold morning, what is the pigeon doing?

activities.title: Be a Sunbird: reach the juice at the bottom
activities.context: In this activity you try to drink juice from the bottom of a tall, narrow bottle, the way a sunbird reaches the sweet juice deep inside a flower.

materials.item: a tall, narrow bottle or a tall glass
a little juice or water, about 2 spoons

schedule.what: Try to reach the juice with your tongue, a spoon and a straw.

activities.record: Draw a sunbird with a long, curved beak, reaching into a flower.

setup.art: A tall narrow bottle with a little orange juice at the bottom, next to a spoon and a straw.
setup.caption: 1. Pour a little juice into the bottom of a tall bottle.

setup.art: A child sipping the juice through a straw from the bottle.
setup.caption: 2. Try the spoon. Then try the straw, like a long beak.

flow.do: Pour about 2 spoons of juice into the bottle. Ask your child how they could drink it without tipping the bottle.
flow.say: The juice is at the very bottom. You must not tip the bottle. How can you reach it?
flow.kid: Can you reach the juice without tipping the bottle?

ask.q: How can you reach the juice without tipping the bottle?

flow.do: Let your child try a spoon first, then the straw.
flow.say: Try the spoon. Now try the straw. Which works best? Why?
flow.kid: Try the spoon. Then try the straw. Which works?
flow.parent: A teaspoon should not reach the juice. If it does, use a taller, narrower bottle.

flow.do: Tell your child about the sunbird: she has a long, thin, curved beak and sips nectar from deep inside flowers. Ask how her beak is like the straw.
flow.say: A flower keeps the sweet juice, called nectar, deep inside. How does a sunbird reach it?
flow.kid: How is a sunbird's beak like the straw?

check.q: Which beak is best for sipping nectar deep inside a flower?
check.why: A long, thin, curved beak reaches deep into a flower, like the straw reached the bottom of the bottle. A short, thick beak is for cracking seeds.

activities.title: Bird Café: what is good for birds, and what is not?
activities.context: In this activity you sort kitchen foods into good and bad for birds. Then you put out a bowl of water and a few grains, and check the next day who came.

materials.item: a shallow bowl, such as a clay saucer or a steel plate with a rim
a pinch of grains such as broken rice, bajra or ragi
a green paper and a red paper, or any two sheets with GOOD and NOT GOOD written on them
a few kitchen foods to sort: rice, a biscuit, a slice of banana, a chip, a pinch of salt

activities.safety: A grown-up places the bowl, inside the balcony railing or on a sill with a grill. Never lean out of a window.

schedule.what: Sort the foods. Put out a shallow bowl of water and a pinch of grains.
Check the bowl and grains. Change the water. Who came?

activities.record: Draw your bird café. Draw any bird you saw, or any sign, like a feather or droppings.

setup.art: Kitchen foods on a table in two groups: rice, banana and bajra on a green paper, a chip, a biscuit and salt on a red paper.
setup.caption: 1. Sort the foods: good for birds, or not.

setup.art: A shallow clay saucer of water and a few grains on a balcony floor inside the railing.
setup.caption: 2. Put out water and a pinch of grains.

flow.do: Put a green paper and a red paper on the table. Your child sorts the foods: green for good for birds, red for not good.
flow.say: Which of these foods are good for a bird? Which could make a bird ill? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put good bird food on green. Put bad bird food on red.

ask.q: Why is the chip not good for a bird?

flow.parent: Grains, plain cooked rice and cut fruit are fine in small amounts. Salty, spicy, sugary and fried foods are not. Biscuits and bread fill a bird up but give little of what a bird needs.

flow.do: Fill the shallow bowl with clean water. Put it and a small pinch of grains where birds can land and you can watch.
flow.say: Birds need water every day, to drink and to bathe. Where should we put the bowl?
flow.kid: Put the bowl where birds can land. Can you see it from inside?

flow.do: Next day, look at the bowl and the grains. Tip out the old water, rinse the bowl and fill it again.
flow.say: Did anyone come? Are the grains gone? Why must we change the water every day?
flow.kid: Who came to your café? Change the water.

ask.q: Why change the water every day?

flow.parent: Birds may take a few days to find a new bowl. If no bird comes on day 2, that is still a real result. Keep the bowl out and look again. Mosquitoes can breed in water left for a few days, so change it daily.

projects.title: My Window Bird Book
projects.context: In this five-day project you make a small book of the birds you see or hear from your home. Each day you draw one bird, and say what that bird was doing.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled (a grown-up staples) into a little book

schedule.what: Make the book. Watch from a window for 5 minutes and draw the first bird.
Watch for 5 minutes. Draw a bird and the bird's beak.
Watch for 5 minutes. Draw what a bird was doing: eating, calling, flying or resting.
Listen with eyes closed. Draw the bird you heard.
Finish the cover. Show your book to someone at home and tell them about each page.

projects.record: One page for each day: the bird, the beak, and what the bird was doing.

setup.art: Three folded sheets stapled into a small book, with 'My Window Birds' written on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and staple paper into a little book.

setup.art: A child at a window drawing a myna in the book, with the real myna on a wire outside.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, draw one bird you saw or heard.

flow.do: 1. Fold the book. A grown-up staples it. 2. Write the title together. 3. Watch from a window for 5 minutes. 4. Your child draws the first bird.
flow.say: Let's make a book of our window birds. Which bird can you see? What colour is the beak?
flow.kid: Make your bird book. Watch the window. Draw a bird.
flow.parent: If you see no bird, draw one you heard, or a bird you have seen before from this window. Crows and pigeons are nearly always about.

flow.do: On days 2, 3 and 4, watch or listen for 5 minutes and add one page each day.
flow.say: What was the bird doing? Eating, calling, flying or resting?
flow.kid: Watch the bird. What is the bird doing? Draw the bird.

flow.do: On day 5, your child makes the cover. Then they show the book to someone at home and tell them about each page.
flow.say: Tell me about your bird book. Which bird did you like best? Why?
flow.kid: Show your book and tell about each page. Which bird was your favourite?

challenges.title: Stitch a Cradle Like a Tailorbird
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A tailorbird sews leaves together to hide the nest. You make a leaf cradle that holds two chana as eggs, using thread and no glue.
challenges.problem: Make a cradle from leaves or paper leaves that holds two chana 'eggs'. The eggs must not fall out when you tip the cradle a little. Use thread, not glue or tape.
constraints: The two chana must stay in the cradle when you tip it gently.
Use leaves, or leaf shapes cut from paper.
materials: 2 leaf shapes cut from paper (or 2 big leaves from a potted plant, if you can spare them)
2 chana or small beans for eggs
general: A tailorbird pokes holes along the edges of a leaf with her sharp beak.
She pulls plant thread or spider silk through the holes, and ties knots so the thread holds.
Inside the cone of leaves, she builds a soft cup of grass and fluff.
creative: Fold one big leaf into a cone and stitch only one side.
Stitch three small leaves into a bowl.
Line the cradle with cotton wool, like the soft cup inside a real nest.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own cradle. Test it by tipping it a little. If an egg falls out, change one thing and try again.

setup.art: Two green leaves with a row of pencil holes along one edge, and a strand of wool beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Poke holes along the edges of two leaves.

setup.art: Two leaves stitched together with wool into a cone, with two chana resting inside.
setup.caption: 2. Stitch them together. Put in two chana eggs and tip gently.

flow.do: Tell your child how a tailorbird sews leaves into a cradle with her beak and thread.
flow.say: A tailorbird sews two leaves together with her beak. How could we do that with thread?
flow.kid: A tailorbird sews leaves. How could you sew them?

flow.do: 1. Cut two leaf shapes from paper. A grown-up helps poke holes with a pencil tip. 2. Your child pushes the wool through the holes. A grown-up ties the knots. 3. Put in two chana.
flow.say: Where do the holes need to go? How will the knots stop the thread coming out?
flow.kid: Poke holes. Push the wool through. Ask for help with the knot.

good: So the thread doesn't slip out.

flow.parent: Paper tears if holes are too close to the edge. Put them about one finger-width in. Twist the end of the wool tight so it goes through a hole easily.

flow.do: Tip the cradle gently. If an egg falls out, ask your child what to change.
flow.say: Tip it gently. Did the eggs stay? What could you change?
flow.kid: Tip your cradle gently. Did the eggs stay in?
flow.think: How does a tiny bird do all this with only a beak and two feet?

items.p: Circle the birds. Cross out the animals who are not birds.
items.why: Hens, peacocks and ostriches have feathers, so they are birds. A bat and a cat have fur, and a butterfly is an insect.
items.art: Six small pictures: a hen, a bat, a peacock, a butterfly, an ostrich and a cat.

items.p: Draw a line from each beak to the food.
items.why: A thick beak cracks seeds, a long curved beak reaches into flowers, and a long sharp beak grabs slippery fish.
items.art: Three bird heads on the left, and seeds, a flower and a fish on the right.

items.p: Draw a bird. Colour the feathers. Show the beak, two wings and two legs.
items.a: A bird with feathers, a beak, two wings and two legs.
items.why: A strong drawing shows all four parts every bird has: feathers, a beak, two wings and two legs.
items.art: An empty box with a branch drawn at the bottom for the bird to sit on.

items.p: A bird sitting on her nest hears another bird's danger call. Why does she press down flat and stay still?
items.why: The danger call warns that a cat or other hunter is near. Pressing flat and staying still makes her hard to see.

items.p: In the experiment A Bean for Every Call, you dropped a bean in a cup for every bird call. Draw the three cups. Draw the beans from each cup in a line underneath.
items.a: Three lines of beans of different lengths, labelled morning, afternoon and evening.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the longest line under the time with the most calls, as the child found.
items.art: Three empty cups drawn in a row with space under each one.

items.p: A bird uses a nest to keep the eggs and chicks safe.
items.why: True. Most birds build a nest when it is time to lay eggs, and leave it when the chicks have flown.

items.p: Write what each feather does: fly or keep warm.
items.why: Stiff wing feathers push on the air. Fluffy feathers hold warm air next to the bird's skin.
items.art: A long stiff feather and a small fluffy feather, each with an empty line beside it.

items.p: Draw a line from each bird to the nest.
pairs: A nest of sticks in a tree
A few twigs on a ledge
items.why: Crows pile up sticks, tailorbirds stitch leaves, and pigeons make a small, loose pile of twigs.
items.art: A crow, a tailorbird and a pigeon on the left, and three nests on the right.

items.p: A crow calls loudly and other crows fly to her. What might she be saying? Tell a grown-up, who writes your answer down.
items.a: She might be saying 'danger', or 'come here', or 'there is food'.
items.why: A strong answer says the call is a message, and gives a reason from what the other crows did.

items.p: Two friends see a baby bird hopping on the ground under a tree.

views.says: Let's pick the baby up and take the baby home to look after.
Let's leave the baby. The parents are probably close by.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one good thing about the other friend's idea.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, such as 'The second friend, because the parents are still feeding the chick.' Then it is fair to the first friend, who wants to keep the chick safe from cats.
items.why: A chick hopping on the ground is often learning to fly, and the parents still feed the chick. Watching from far away is usually best. If the chick is hurt, a grown-up can call a bird rescue group.

items.p: Which of these is NOT a job that feathers do?
opts: Help a bird see in the dark
items.why: Feathers help a bird fly, keep warm, keep dry and show colours. They do not help a bird see.

items.p: Draw a pigeon on a cold morning and a pigeon on a hot afternoon.
items.a: A round, fluffed-up pigeon for the cold morning, and a thin, sleek pigeon for the hot afternoon.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the fluffed-up feathers in the cold, because fluffing holds more warm air.

items.p: Juice is at the bottom of a tall, thin bottle. Why can a straw reach it when a spoon cannot?
opts: The straw is long and thin
items.why: A long, thin straw reaches deep into the bottle, as a sunbird's long, thin beak reaches deep into a flower.

items.p: When you count bird calls, why is it better to drop a bean for each call than just to remember? Tell a grown-up, who writes your answer down.
items.a: Because you can count the beans afterwards and compare the cups. Remembering is hard.
items.why: A strong answer says the beans keep a true count we can see and compare later.

items.p: Colour the good bird foods green and the bad ones red.
items.why: Water, grains and fruit are good. Salty, sugary and spicy foods can make birds ill.

items.p: Put the story The Bulbuls in the Money Plant in order.
items: Two eggs appear in the nest
a: Two eggs appear in the nest
items.why: Birds build the nest first, then lay eggs, then the eggs hatch, then the chicks grow feathers and fly.
items.art: Four small pictures, mixed up: an empty grass nest, two spotted eggs, two pink chicks, chicks flying.

items.p: You drop beans for bird calls: 5 in the first minute and 3 in the next minute. How many calls did you hear in the two minutes?
items.why: 5 and 3 more make 8. Each bean is one call.

items.p: A crow has a strong beak and eats almost anything. Why is that useful in a city? Tell a grown-up, who writes your answer down.
items.a: In a city a crow can find grain, scraps, insects and fruit, and her strong beak can eat all of them. She will not go hungry if one food is gone.
items.why: A crow can eat many foods, so she can live where food changes. A strong beak is the tool that makes this work.

items.p: Today, only birds have feathers.
items.why: True. Today no other animal has feathers. Bats and insects fly without them.

items.p: Two sisters talk about the pigeons on their balcony.

views.says: Let's put out lots of grain every day, so the pigeons are never hungry.
Let's only put out water, so not too many pigeons come.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For the older sister: the grain helps the birds. For the younger sister: too many pigeons push other birds away, and the droppings can make people ill. Then the child is fair to the other side.
items.why: This is a real argument. Feeding helps some birds, but feeding a lot in one place can bring huge flocks of one kind. Water in summer helps every kind of bird.

videos.title: The dawn chorus in an Indian city: birds calling at sunrise
videos.why: Lets the child hear many Indian city birds calling at once, to compare with what they heard in the experiment A Bean for Every Call.
videos.check: Find a real recording made in India at sunrise. Check the birds named are the ones heard.

videos.title: A tailorbird sewing leaves into a nest
videos.why: Shows how a tailorbird stitches leaves, which is hard to see in real life. The challenge Stitch a Cradle Like a Tailorbird copies this stitching.
videos.check: Found by search: "Tailorbird nest sewing like pro" by Life On Planet Earth, 3 min. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: A close look at bird feathers
videos.why: Gives a close look at a feather, which a home magnifier cannot show as well.
videos.check: Found by search: "Look Closely at Feathers | Nat Geo Kids Birds Playlist" by Nat Geo Kids, 1 min. A parent may preview it.

quiz.why: Every bird has feathers. Birds have no teeth, and fur belongs to animals like cats and bats.

quiz.p: A bat can fly. Is a bat a bird?
opts: No, because a bat has no feathers
quiz.why: A bat has fur, not feathers. Flying does not make an animal a bird.

quiz.p: What do soft, fluffy feathers do for a bird?
quiz.why: Fluffy feathers hold warm air close to the skin, like a blanket.

quiz.p: A sparrow has a short, thick beak. What does a sparrow mostly eat?
quiz.why: A short, thick beak is strong enough to crack seeds and grains.

quiz.p: Why does a bird build a nest?
opts: To keep the eggs and chicks safe
To hide from the rain every night of the year
quiz.why: A nest is a cradle for eggs and chicks. Most birds sleep on branches when they are not nesting.

quiz.p: How does a tailorbird make a nest?
opts: She digs a hole in the ground
quiz.why: A tailorbird pokes holes in leaves with her beak and stitches them with plant thread or spider silk.

quiz.p: You drop one bean into a cup each time you hear a bird call. What does one bean stand for?
quiz.why: One bean drops for every call. So more beans means more calls.

quiz.p: A bulbul gives a fast, sharp call when a cat comes near. What does the call mean?
quiz.why: A fast, sharp call when a cat comes near is an alarm call. Other birds hide when they hear it.

quiz.p: Which is the best thing to give birds on a hot summer day?
opts: A shallow bowl of clean water
quiz.why: Birds need water to drink and bathe. In summer, city birds can find it hard to get water. Salty and sweet snacks can make them ill.

quiz.p: Why should you change the water in a bird bowl every day?
opts: So it stays clean and mosquitoes cannot breed
quiz.why: Old water gets dirty, and mosquitoes can lay eggs in still water left for days.

applications: Bird watchers count birds every year to see which kinds are growing in number and which are going down.
Scientists study how young birds learn songs, to understand how children learn to talk.
Families put out clay bowls of water for birds in the hot months.
In Assam, the scientist Purnima Devi Barman and a group of village women protect the trees where greater adjutant storks nest.

spotted.art: Five crows on an electric wire against a pale morning sky, beaks open.

spotted.text: A koel calling 'ku-oo' louder and louder from a tree in Chennai or Delhi in April and May.
spotted.art: A shiny black male koel with red eyes, half hidden in a mango tree.

spotted.text: Pigeons fluffed up into round balls on a ledge on a winter morning in Lucknow or Pune.
spotted.art: Three round, fluffed-up grey pigeons on a window ledge with mist behind them.

spotted.text: A purple sunbird sipping from hibiscus flowers on a balcony in Bengaluru.
spotted.art: A tiny shiny purple sunbird with a curved beak at a red hibiscus flower.

spotted.text: A big crowd of parakeets and mynas calling in a tree before dark, in Hyderabad or Kolkata.
spotted.art: A big tree at dusk full of green parakeets and brown mynas, with sound lines everywhere.

open_questions.q: Why do birds sing most at dawn?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas. Sound may carry far in the still morning air, or it may be too dark to find food, so birds sing instead. Nobody is sure.

open_questions.q: What does a bird feel when singing?
open_questions.why_open: Birds sense, choose and remember. But nobody knows what singing feels like to a bird from the inside.

open_questions.q: How much do birds understand of each other's calls?
open_questions.why_open: We know birds react to some calls, even calls of other kinds of birds. We do not yet know how much they understand.

ask_kids: Which bird did you hear first today? What do you think that bird was saying?
Is that bird fluffed up or sleek today? Is the weather warm or cold?
What shape is that bird's beak? What do you think the bird eats?
Where could a bird build a nest in our building?
Which bird near our home is the loudest? Where does that bird sit?

jokes.j: Why do birds wake up so early?
jokes.a: Because the early bird gets the worm!

jokes.j: What do you call a bird who is afraid to fly?
Why did the crow sit on the phone wire?
Which bird is always out of breath?
Why did the pigeon fluff up?
What do you give a sick bird?
What does a bird say when she builds a nest?
Why was the tailorbird so tidy?
jokes.a: She always had things sewn up!

maths.problem: In the bean test, you drop a bean in a cup for every bird call. The morning cup has 12 beans and the afternoon cup has 4 beans. Which time had more calls? Why do you think so?
maths.explain: 12 is more than 4. Many birds call most in the early morning, and rest in the afternoon heat.
maths.context: This is about the bean test, where you dropped a bean for every bird call.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers tells us when the birds were busiest calling.

maths.problem: A bulbul laid 2 eggs. A crow laid 4 eggs. How many eggs in all?
maths.context: This is about birds' eggs in their nests.
maths.why_maths: Adding tells us how many chicks might hatch in the two nests.

maths.problem: A tally of birds seen from a window shows: crows ||||, pigeons |||, a sunbird |. Which bird was seen most? If one more sunbird is seen, will sunbirds catch up with the crows?
maths.answer: Crows, 4 times. No: with one more, sunbirds would be 2, still less than 4.
maths.explain: 4 tally marks for crows is the most. 1 and 1 more is 2, and 2 is less than 4.
maths.context: This is about watching birds from a window for the bird book.
maths.why_maths: A tally keeps count as birds come and go, and lets us predict what one more would change.

warmup.a: To hold warm air close to the body.
To keep eggs and chicks safe.

founder: ideas/by_topic/the-world-of-birds.md: evolution picture book and species ladder (birds from dinosaurs, about 150 million years ago); kept for Level 4, nothing used at this level.
science: Feathers are found only in living birds; all birds have beaks, lay eggs and have no teeth (any ornithology text).
Feather structure: barbs with barbules and hooklets that re-zip when preened; down traps air for insulation; birds moult.
Dawn chorus: the peak of bird song around sunrise; the cause is still debated (acoustic transmission, low light for foraging, and other ideas).
Song learning: W. H. Thorpe, chaffinches reared in isolation sang abnormal songs (1950s).
Compositional syntax in Japanese tit calls: Suzuki, Wheatcroft and Griesser, Nature Communications, 2016.
Common tailorbird (Orthotomus sutorius) stitches leaf edges with plant fibre or spider silk; red-vented bulbuls nest in shrubs and balcony plants, lay 2 to 3 spotted eggs.
House crows in Indian cities use wire and metal hangers in nests; red-wattled lapwings lay eggs on bare ground and flat roofs.

Margaret Morse Nice: song sparrow study on the Olentangy River floodplain, Columbus, Ohio, from 1928, with coloured leg bands; about 870 birds trapped (Bird Observer, 2020; The Nature Conservancy blog, 2016).
Purnima Devi Barman and the Hargila Army protecting greater adjutant nesting trees in Assam (Whitley Award 2017, UNEP Champions of the Earth 2022).
Most birds do not abandon chicks touched by people (widely stated by bird rescue and ornithology groups).
Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1 (also Rig Veda 1.164.20): two birds on one tree. Farid ud-Din Attar, Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds), about 1177.

roots.context: In the experiment A Bean for Every Call, we listened to the birds outside our window and counted their calls. Now we ask what all that calling tells us about birds, and about us.

deep_truth.truth: When one crow calls loudly, other crows look, fly over or go quiet. The call changed what they did. So a bird call is a message, and the birds who hear it understand it.
deep_truth.habit: We call bird sounds 'chirping' or 'noise', as if they meant nothing. But birds act on each other's calls. So the calls are messages from one living being to another.
deep_truth.evidence: At your window, watch what the other crows do when one crow calls. In the experiment A Bean for Every Call, you also listened for birds answering each other.

three.who_am_i: You learned to talk by listening to the people around you. A young bird learns to sing by listening too.
three.what_is_life: A bird's day is full: finding food, calling to friends, warning of danger and caring for chicks.
three.what_is_this_world: The air outside your window is full of messages between birds. We hear only a few of them.

roots.thread: Every bird has the same few parts: feathers, a beak, two wings and two legs. There are about 11,000 kinds of birds, and more than 1,300 of them live in India. Each kind has a different beak, nest and call, so each lives in a different way.

teachings.teaching: Two birds sit on the same tree. One bird eats the fruit. The other bird does not eat, and only watches.
teachings.link: In the experiment A Bean for Every Call, you sat still and only listened, like the watching bird. Just listening let you notice the birds talking.

teachings.source: Farid ud-Din Attar, The Conference of the Birds (Mantiq al-Tayr), about 1177
teachings.teaching: In the Persian poem The Conference of the Birds, written by Attar, the birds of the world meet, talk together and set off on a long journey as one flock.
teachings.link: Real birds call to each other and gather together too, as crows, mynas and parakeets do in big trees before dark.

science.text: Many birds learn their songs by listening to grown-up birds, as human babies learn to talk.
Japanese tits put two calls together in a set order, and other tits understand the order. Whether any bird has a language like ours is still argued about.

other_view.view: They say only humans have a true language. Bird calls carry a few messages, like danger or food, but birds cannot put calls together to say endless new things, as people do with words.

practice.title: Be the watching bird
practice.say: Sit by the window. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly. Listen for the farthest bird you can hear. Now listen for the nearest one. Is any bird answering another? Open your eyes slowly.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Breathe slowly. Find the farthest bird. Find the nearest bird. Is anyone answering?

ask: If birds are talking all day, what do you think they talk about?
Would a bird think our talking is just noise?
Who taught you your first words? Who teaches a young bird to sing?
roots.art: A child sitting very still by a window with eyes closed, and two birds on a branch outside, one eating a fruit and one watching.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that birds of one kind are not all alike? This card tells the true story of a woman who watched the birds near her home.
how_we_found_out.story: About a hundred years ago, many bird experts studied dead birds kept in museum drawers. A small brown bird in a backyard seemed to have little to teach. Margaret Morse Nice thought differently. She lived in Columbus, a city in America, and had no job at a university. From 1928, she studied the song sparrows by the river below her home. She caught the birds gently and put tiny coloured rings on their legs. Each bird got a different set of colours, so she could tell them apart. Over about eight years she ringed hundreds of birds and watched them again and again. She found that each male sang his own set of songs, and guarded his own patch of ground. Some birds stayed all winter, and some flew away and came back. No two sparrows lived in the same way. Other scientists later said her work started a new way of studying birds: watching living birds, one by one.
how_we_found_out.who: Margaret Morse Nice, an American scientist who studied song sparrows from her home
how_we_found_out.when: From 1928, for about eight years; her books on the song sparrow came out in 1937 and 1943
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought you could learn what you needed about a kind of bird from dead birds in a museum, as if every bird of that kind were the same. Nice put coloured rings on living birds and watched them for years. She showed that each male had his own songs and his own patch of ground, and lived a life different from the next.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman in a 1930s dress kneeling by a river bank, gently holding a small brown sparrow with coloured rings on the legs.

playtest: Walked through both games with 2 and 4 players, each activity, the bean test and the bird book in a city flat. Fixed: game win and tie rule, wrong cards go to the bottom of the pile, bean rule agrees with the parent tip, morning timing in the steps, a guess that treated a debated idea as fact, 'read your book' for a child who cannot read yet, a maths question missing its morning cup, an unchecked claim about doctors, a repeated 'who answers' question, and a deep truth that leaned on the made-up story. Videos are still to find (the validator needs 3).

quiz: An animal that flies is always a bird.
A bat flies but has fur; feathers are what make a bird.
An ostrich cannot fly, but an ostrich is still a bird.
An ostrich has feathers, and feathers make a bird.
The shape of a bird's beak fits the food that bird eats.
Different foods need different beaks.
Birds have teeth to chew their food.
Birds have no teeth; the beak picks up, holds and breaks the food.
Most birds sleep in their nests all year.
Most birds use a nest only for eggs and chicks, and sleep on branches.
Bird calls are only noise and mean nothing.
One call can mean danger, another food, and other birds act on them.
If a person touches a baby bird, the mother will always leave the chick.
Most birds do not leave a chick for that, but it is best to leave the chick alone.
Birds need clean water every day.
Water keeps birds healthy, in summer most of all.
Many young birds learn their songs by listening, as children learn to talk.
They copy the birds around them.
Birds sing to tell other birds 'this place is mine'.
Singing also helps a bird find a partner.
odd: The others have feathers, but a bat has fur.

The others are safe for birds; salty food can make birds ill.
The others can fly, but an ostrich cannot, even though an ostrich has wings.
